title: Working holiday visa changes driving backpackers away, employers say
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Working holiday visa changes driving backpackers away, employers say

Industry leaders say backpackers are already leaving sectors that are heavily reliant on them because of federal government's planned changes to the working holiday visa.

Topic:Migration Policy

Many backpackers are weighing their options after the federal government announced changes for working holiday-makers, employers say. (Flickr CC BY-NC-ND 2.0: Jo Christian Oterhals)

Far North Queensland industries are already losing staff due to working holiday visa changes, major employers say.

The changes being rolled out over the next 12 months will cap the number of working holiday-makers from certain countries.

The federal government says Pacific workers will help to fill the gap.

In Far North Queensland the school holiday tourist season is booming but businesses fear they will not be able to keep up with demand in future.

Following the federal government's changes to working holiday visas, Crystalbrook Collection chief executive Geoff York said his staff were already hesitant to stay.

"We've had some second-year working holiday-makers leave already," he said.

Geoff York says he is already seeing the effects of the proposed changes on his workforce. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

Mr York said 45 per cent of the company's 500 employees across its Cairns hotels, restaurants, bars and day spa were on working holiday visas.

But he said many of those workers would not risk another six months of regional work to "potentially qualify" for the third-year ballot.

"It's a one in six chance that you'll qualify, so that's not good," Mr York said.

He said the industry could face shortages similar to those experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic and that operating at full capacity would not be possible despite "tremendous demand".

"I've got two 300-room hotels and I may only be able to fill it to 250 rooms," Mr York said.

Backpackers wanting a second-year working holiday visa must work 88 days in regional or remote Australia.

Under the changes progressively being rolled out over the next 12 months, 462 visas will be capped, and applicants will have to enter a ballot when applying for first, second and third-year visas.

Mark Olsen says the diversity of languages spoken by working holiday visa holders is important for adventure tourism safety. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

Tourism Tropical North Queensland said the industry in northern Australia wanted the government to scrap the changes.

"It is our school holidays — this is one of our peak seasons and we've got staff who are leaving the region," chief executive Mark Olsen said.

He said working holiday-makers from various countries brought language skills that helped keep visitors safe.

"Whether that's skydiving, bungee jumping, diving, snorkelling, whitewater rafting, we need to be able to speak to them effectively in their language," he said.

Mr Olsen said the industry also relied on workers staying long enough to build skills in roles such as dive masters.

He said the argument for housing was not relevant in the Far North.

"Ninety per cent of their accommodation is in a hostel or on a farm, so they are not a significant contributor to a housing shortage," Mr Olsen said.

Cairns Chamber of Commerce CEO Patricia O'Neil said the cuts would also be "devastating" for aged care, childcare, labour and construction.

Patricia O'Neill says backpackers are an important component of the local economy. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

FNQ Growers president Joe Moro said the government had "basically terminated the whole process of the working holiday visa" for the farming sector.

He said working holiday-makers made up about a third of the 15,000 workers on Far North Queensland farms.

As Australia's "third-biggest fruit bowl", growers relied on the international visitors to fill gaps during peak harvests, Mr Moro said.

He said workers would be less willing to do the "hard work" on farms for six months when a third year was not guaranteed, preferring to visit the region as tourists.
